Your domain reputation follows you Your IP reputation changes Your sending history doesn’t move on its own Use cases · Migration ESP Migration ESP How do I switch ESP without losing deliverability? ¾ of your reputation comes with you, and ¼ doesn’t. Talk to a deliverability expert That asymmetry is what breaks migrations. Your domain reputation follows you Your IP reputation changes Your sending history doesn’t move on its own 01 – What moves with you 02 – What breaks migrations 03 – One first impression 04 – How an expert plans it 05 – Email Deliverability Consulting Services 06 – Client results and testimonials 07 – Switching ESP FAQ Sending full volume on day one looks exactly like a spammer A migration rarely fails because of the platform. It fails because of poor scheduling and sending behavior. Placement dropped the week you switched New IPs with no history, full volume from day one. Fine at Gmail, throttled at Microsoft Providers warm up at different speeds. Bounces spiked on the first full send Your suppression list didn’t come with you. Both platforms are still sending Two sources, one domain, inconsistent signals. You migrated to fix a problem, and it followed Domain reputation moved with the domain. Weeks in, and it still hasn’t recovered No baseline was measured, so nobody can say by how much. Any of these will cost you deliverability and delivery quality Each signal tells providers the same thing: this sender arrived from nowhere and behaves unpredictably. Several are usually true at once, and the damage typically happens in the first two weeks. The easiest problems to prevent, and the most expensive to undo. 01 Full volume on day one The fastest way to burn a new IP: providers read a sudden ramp from an unknown source as snowshoe spam. 02 Warm-up compressed into a week Most senders need 4 to 8 weeks end-to-end, ramping 25–35% per send. Rushing it sets a ceiling you then spend months climbing back from. 03 Suppression lists left behind Unsubscribes, hard bounces, and complainers rarely export cleanly across platforms, so they get mailed again — the fastest route to a spike in complaints. 04 Authentication not migrated cleanly Every platform signs with its own DKIM keys, and an SPF record that still includes the old ESP can exceed the lookup limit. 05 Dedicated IP at too low a volume Below roughly 100K sends a month, the signal is too thin, and the IP goes cold between campaigns. 06 Two platforms sending at once Same audience, same domain, unaligned authentication — duplicate sends and contradictory signals. 07 New tracking or link domain Tracking domains carry their own reputation — a brand-new one is unvouched for on every message. 08 Migrating to escape a problem Domain reputation follows the domain. You arrive with the same damage, plus a cold-start problem. Recognize one of these problems? We solve them every day Our senior consultants have fixed exactly these issues for 500+ brands. A migration often overlaps with these closely related problems. See how we fix it Explore all deliverability challenges Switching ESP: FAQ My deliverability dropped after switching ESP. Can it be fixed? Yes, and the sooner the better. A slight dip in the first sends from new IPs is normal; a decline that hasn’t recovered after three or four weeks is not. It means either the ramp outpaced the trust you’d earned, or something didn’t move with you. The usual culprits are a suppression list left behind, DKIM signing on the new platform that never aligned with your domain, or volume raised faster than providers could absorb. All three are recoverable, but the fix is a controlled re-ramp on your engaged segment, not more sending. Will changing ESP fix my deliverability problem? Almost never on its own, and it often makes things worse. Domain reputation travels with your domain, so a migration carries the existing problem into the new stack while adding cold IPs on top. For most senders, deliverability issues come from sending behavior, not the platform. Find and fix the cause first, then migrate. A new platform buys you better tooling, not a clean slate. Does my sender reputation transfer to the new ESP? Most of it does. Domain reputation follows your domain everywhere, for better or worse. IP reputation doesn’t: on new IPs, you start from zero. That asymmetry is why migrations go wrong — senders assume everything resets, when the only part that resets is the one that was protecting them. How long does IP warm-up take? Plan 4 to 8 weeks end-to-end, longer if you send more than a few million emails a month. The schedule matters more than the duration: start with your most engaged recipients, raise volume by roughly 25–35% per send, and hold at each level until placement is stable. Compressing warm-up into a week is the single most common migration failure. Should I use a dedicated or a shared IP after migrating? It depends on volume, not preference. A dedicated IP only builds reputation if you send consistently enough to keep it warm. Below roughly 100,000 emails a month, the signal is too thin, and you’re better off on a well-managed shared pool. Asking for a dedicated IP at low volume is a common and expensive mistake. Should I change my domain when I change ESP? Generally, no. A fresh domain abandons whatever positive history you had and presents providers with an unknown sender suddenly sending volume — itself a spam signal. A subdomain of your existing domain is usually the right answer: it inherits organizational trust while keeping streams separate. Rule of thumb: only change domains when your website domain changes too (a rebrand, an acquisition, or a merger). Migrate without paying for it in the inbox Whether the move is next month or three weeks away, our consultants will measure where you stand, tell you what actually transfers, and size the ramp your volume requires.
